score is how far the text is from conforming, not a confidence value. Here it is good / total over the twelve letters the pack could see against z: two hits out of twelve chances is 10/12 ≈ 0.833. What good and total count differs by procedure — letters for a lipogram, lines for a metrical form, words for a lexical one — so compare scores within a procedure, not across procedures.

Each entry in violations is where and how the text failed: rule names which check tripped, offset is the character position in the original text (or null when a violation is not localisable, such as a form-wide count), found is what was there, and expected is what the rule required. note carries anything else worth saying and is usually null.

metrics is free-form and procedure-specific, but one key recurs across the syllable-counting forms — sonnets, ballades, iambic pentameter and the rest — metrics["estimated_words"]. A pronouncing dictionary does not know every word, and a procedure that needs a syllable count for a word it cannot look up falls back to a spelling-based heuristic rather than refusing to check the line at all. Doing so silently would let a caller believe every count was exact. estimated_words is how the library discloses, instead, how many words in the checked text were guessed rather than looked up — so a caller who needs certainty can decide whether that number is small enough to trust.

docs.title: denckring.core.protocol.Constructive
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

A procedure that can generate, not merely validate.

apply is optional by ADR 0002, so it is not on BaseProcedure. This protocol is how callers ask whether a given procedure has one, and it narrows the type at the same time.

seed was an explicit keyword here and is now an ordinary parameter on SeedParams, carried by the ten procedures that draw. A keyword named in this signature binds before **params and so can never be validated, which is what made seed unvalidatable for all 27.

produce joined apply here for the same reason: runtime_checkable makes isinstance check method presence only, and every ConstructiveProcedure inherits both from the base class, so the set of procedures this protocol matches is unchanged by adding the second name.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: A pack does not declare a language "supported" or not — it declares a capabilities set, built from string constants defined in denckring.lang.base: TOKENS, ALPHABET, FOLD_DIACRITICS, LETTER_SHAPES, SYLLABLES, SYLLABLES_HEURISTIC, SYLLABLES_DICTIONARY, WORDS, NOUNS, GLOSSES, PHONEMES and STRESS. A procedure, in turn, declares a requires list of the same strings on its catalogue entry. BaseProcedure.check compares the two before running anything: if the pack's capabilities do not cover everything the procedure requires, it raises MissingCapability naming the procedure, the language and the missing capability, rather than falling back to an approximation. Adding a language pack is a matter of implementing LanguagePack and declaring which of these strings it can honestly back — nothing more.

A text whose successive lines or words begin with successive letters of the alphabet, from A through to Z.

docs.title: Provenance

• Source: Ancient Hebrew acrostic psalms; Lamentations

  • Checkability: self — decidable from the text and its parameters alone
  • Attested: codified — formulated as a rule by a tradition rather than declared by an author

alliterative_verse · form · validated

Lines split by a caesura in which the stressed syllables of both halves alliterate, rather than rhyming at the end. The checker compares bare first letters: it locates no caesura, reads no stress, and counts "knight" and "king" as alliterating where the Old English metre does not.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The checker compares bare first letters (see the module docstring's own admission that this reads "knight" and "king" as alliterating, which Old English metre would not). German is the sharper case: the tradition this row is named for treats st, sp and sch as staves distinct from a bare s, so a line built on that distinction can pass this checker while failing the tradition, or the reverse. The shipped German fixture is written to hold under both readings rather than relying on the gap.

docs.title: Arca musarithmica
docs.text:
arca_musarithmica · procedural · validated

A box of tablets bearing numbered patterns, chosen by the syllable count and prosodic shape of a phrase, from which a setting is composed. Kircher's own use was musical; the transferable procedure is the one underneath — give a passage its prosodic profile, then draw from a pattern table indexed by that profile.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Athanasius Kircher, Musurgia Universalis (Rome, 1650), book VIII
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind
  • Checkability: source — decidable against the source text it was made from
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: both
  • Languages: en
  • Requires: tokens, syllables.heuristic
  • Deterministic: yes
  • Also known as: musarithmic ark
  • In other languages: Arca musarithmica (de), Arca musarithmica (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Kircher advertises that an amusos — someone with no musical training — can produce correct four-part settings in any language, which is the claim that makes the box interesting. What is implemented here is the indexing, not the counterpoint: a phrase is measured and a pattern drawn from the tablet for its length, and the patterns themselves are never read. Put Kircher's pitch numbers in and you get his machine; put stress patterns or rhyme schemes in and the same bones carry those. No tablet ships. Kircher's own runs to many pages of Musurgia Universalis book VIII and has not been transcribed into anything this project could verify.

docs.title: Prompt hint
docs.text: Count the syllables of the phrase, then take a pattern from the table indexed by that count.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Default Description pinakes string — The pattern tablets, as JSON. source string — The text this one was made from. syntagma string 1 Which tablet to draw from; Kircher's first is plain, his second florid. tonus — None The mode, if the table names any.

docs.text:
ars_combinatoria · permutation · catalogued

A text generated by systematically combining terms drawn from fixed sets, the sets and their order being the whole of the method.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Ramon Llull, Ars Generalis Ultima (1305); named as such by Leibniz (1666)
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind

  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

  • Languages: en

  • Deterministic: yes

  • In other languages: Kombinatorische Kunst (de), Art combinatoire (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: This names a tradition rather than a single procedure: what counts as a valid combination is whatever the particular device specifies, so there is no criterion to check at this level. Its instances are checkable and are catalogued separately — llull_figure, denckring, cent_mille_milliards, wechselsatz.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Georg Philipp Harsdörffer, Deliciae Physico-Mathematicae (Erquickstunden), part two, Nürnberg 1651, XIV. Theil, die IV. Aufgabe, pp. 513-515
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind
  • Checkability: source — decidable against the source text it was made from
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: both
  • Languages: de
  • Requires: tokens, fold_diacritics
  • Deterministic: yes
  • Also known as: Letterwechsel
  • In other languages: Buchstabwechsel (de), Échange de lettres (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Harsdörffer's own synonym is Letterwechsel ("Das Wort Letter für Buchstab / wird in den alten Gedichten hin und wider gefunden", p. 513). Two further rules from the same passage (p. 514) are recorded here, stated but not enforced, because neither is decidable from the checked text alone. Rule I: "Erstlich sollen die Teutschen Namen mit teutschen Endungen den Buchstabwechsel schliessen / wie auch die Lateinischen Namen ihre Endungen behalten: als Johann / Georg. Im Lateinischen Johannes, Georgius etc." — an ending keyed to the name's own language, German or Latin, which this row does not check. Rule III: "Soll der Wechselschluß eine gantze / oder zum wenigsten halbe Meinung geben / welcher das beygesetzte Bild einen vollkommenen Sinn bringet" — the result should give a whole or at least a half sense, completed by an accompanying emblem; whether it does is a judgement no program makes, the same candour antigram's own definition states for opposition of sense. The physical procedure (p. 514) is working method, not an output criterion, and is recorded rather than checked: letters written on paper slips, or on wooden dice because slips "leichtlich verblasen werden" (blow away too easily), with the Stimmer (vowels) separated from the Mitstimmer (consonants) before recombination. Harsdörffer also frames the form as inherently personal — the result "kan keinem gemein seyn als von dessen Namen sie ausgesuchet ist" (can belong to no one but the person whose name it was drawn from) — so source is meant to be a personal name, which this row cannot verify: German capitalises every noun, so capitalisation is no test of namehood. Correction: an earlier draft of this row also claimed that a plain anagram check would wrongly accept a u-for-v or i-for-j swap, and that this was a second, independent reason the row is not a duplicate of anagram. Measured against this codebase, that is false — anagram's fold_diacritics is case-folding plus NFKD combining-mark stripping, which never merged those letters, so anagram already rejects check("anagram", "Uater", lang="de", source="Vater") and check("anagram", "Iohann", lang="de", source="Johann") on its own. The genuine, load-bearing, mutation-tested reason this row exists is the h-exemption alone. The u/i-not-v/j prohibition is still real — Harsdörffer states it, and test_buchstabwechsel.py pins it against a future change to fold_diacritics that might introduce the merge — but it was never a point of difference from anagram, and this note records the correction rather than silently dropping the earlier, wrong claim (the way the llull_figure row records that 504 is the ordered-triple count, not Llull's own).

docs.text: Rearrange every letter of a personal name into another word or words; you may insert or drop an h anywhere, but never write u for v or i for j.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The digit table is a module constant in core/calculator.py, not a pack capability: seven-segment geometry does not vary by orthography the way the ascenders prisoners_constraint reads from letter_shapes do (ADR 0037 D1). 6 and 9 both rotate onto G, so a word containing one has two digit spellings; check accepts either and apply emits 6 (D4), which is why apply is not the byte-for-byte inverse of check for about a third of every corpus. fold_diacritics defaults to false here and to true on every other row (D3): the display cannot write an accent or an ß, so folding would admit words the machine provably cannot show. apply draws from lexicon.graded_words where a pack declares it and from the noun list otherwise, so its corpus differs by language — German declares no graded words at all (ADR 0028), which is why apply_requires names the noun list rather than the richer source (D5).

False by default on this row alone: the display cannot write the accent. require_words boolean True Whether each word must be one the language knows. False checks the display mapping alone, admitting any letter combination it can write. words integer 1 How many words the digits must spell.

docs.title: a-german-poem-the-strips-actually-offer
docs.text:
de — this text satisfies the procedure.

Fünf Scheiben aus Papier, und etwas Zeit.
Ein jeder Ring dreht sich in deiner Hand.
Was hier entsteht, ist selten schon gescheit.
Ein blindes Wort kommt her aus keinem Land.
Hier wird aus Silben Sprache, still gemacht.
Man kann die ganze Sprache darin sehen.
Nicht jedes Drehen hat ein Wort gebracht.
Man läßt die Ringe ihren Weg so gehen.
Am Ende steht ein einzig klares Wort.
Die Scheiben drehen weiter, ganz allein.
Man dreht es immer weiter, immer fort.
Ein Wort ist manchmal nichts als leerer Schein.
Fünf Ringe tragen jeden deutschen Reim.
Und was sie sagen, bleibt zuletzt geheim.

Parameters: source='Fünf Scheiben aus Papier, und etwas Zeit. | Der Denckring liegt geheftet, drehbereit. | Ein Blättlein hält die Sprache, schmal und weit.\nEin jeder Ring dreht sich in deiner Hand. | Die Silben stehen sauber Rand an Rand. | Ein Wort entsteht ganz ohne Verstand.\nWas hier entsteht, ist selten schon gescheit. | Der Zufall kennt kein Maß und auch kein Leid. | Die Ringe schweigen, führen keinen Streit.\nEin blindes Wort kommt her aus keinem Land. | Die Scheiben hält ein dünnes, festes Band. | Die Lettern stehen dicht wie eine Wand.\nHier wird aus Silben Sprache, still gemacht. | Man dreht die Ringe einmal, eine Nacht. | Ein Wort hat über nichts und niemand Macht.\nMan kann die ganze Sprache darin sehen. | Und jeder Ring will für sich selber drehen. | Fünf Scheiben, die nun übereinander stehen.\nNicht jedes Drehen hat ein Wort gebracht. | Der Meister hat das Blättlein wohl bedacht. | Die Sprache liegt hier ohne alle Pracht.\nMan läßt die Ringe ihren Weg so gehen. | Es kann in einem Dreh ein Wort geschehen. | Und keiner muß das blinde Wort verstehen.\nAm Ende steht ein einzig klares Wort. | Und niemand weiß, von welchem stillen Ort. | Was blind war, wird auf einmal lesbar dort.\nDie Scheiben drehen weiter, ganz allein. | Ein Wort kann groß und dennoch nichtig sein. | Der Ring ist alt, das Blättlein ist nur klein.\nMan dreht es immer weiter, immer fort. | Die Sprache liegt im Blättlein wie ein Hort. | Ein totes Wort ist stumm und bald verdorrt.\nEin Wort ist manchmal nichts als leerer Schein. | Der Reim fällt selten glatt und selten rein. | Die Lettern sind gestochen scharf und fein.\nFünf Ringe tragen jeden deutschen Reim. | In jeder Silbe liegt ein ganzer Keim. | Man trägt die ganze Sprache mit nach heim.\nUnd was sie sagen, bleibt zuletzt geheim. | Fünf Scheiben halten sich mit etwas Leim. | So bleibt die ganze Sprache hier daheim.'

Source: constructed example; the fourteen strips are the German set written for the "Cent mille milliards de poèmes" stage scene, copied here verbatim. text is the first alternative at every position — the catalogue's own languages: [en, de] for this row needs at least one German case behind it (test_declared_languages_have_a_fixture), and a real 14-position poem, not a shortened stand-in, is what actually exercises the shape the row claims. The German pack ships no phonemes, so this only confirms that each line is one the strips offer — not that the poem rhymes; see the stage's own test for that limitation stated in full.

docs.title: hopkins-pied-beauty-curtal
docs.text:
en — this text does not satisfy the procedure.

Glory be to God for dappled things —
  For skies of couple-colour as a brinded cow;
    For rose-moles all in stipple upon trout that swim;
Fresh-firecoal chestnut-falls; finches' wings;
  Landscape plotted and pieced — fold, fallow, and plough;
    And áll trádes, their gear and tackle and trim.
All things counter, original, spare, strange;
  Whatever is fickle, freckled (who knows how?)
    With swift, slow; sweet, sour; adazzle, dim;
He fathers-forth whose beauty is past change:
                  Praise him.

Source: Gerard Manley Hopkins, "Pied Beauty" (written 1877; first published in Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins, ed. Robert Bridges, 1918), his own coinage of the form. Rejected: the poem is in sprung rhythm, which curtal_sonnet's catalogue note (ADR 0040 D4) says it does not read — the syllabic model expects a steady count and iambic stress per line, and sprung rhythm packs variable numbers of unstressed syllables around a fixed stress count instead. That mismatch produces 7 wrong_line_length violations (lines running 9 to 12 syllables, and the closing half-line "Praise him." at 2) and 4 wrong_stress violations on "chestnut", "tackle", "counter/original", and "sour". Measured on this HEAD: score 0.8878, 11 violations.

docs.title: Dactylic hexameter
docs.text:
dactylic_hexameter · form · validated

Six feet, each a dactyl or a spondee, the fifth almost always a dactyl. Read as accentual verse, stress standing in for the classical quantity English has not got; the fifth foot is fixed as a dactyl and the caesura is not checked.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Traditional; the metre of Homer and Virgil
  • Attribution: traditional — classical or folk; no single origin to name

docs.title: Details
docs.text:

  • Deterministic: yes
  • In other languages: Hexameter (de), Hexamètre dactylique (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Checked as English accentual verse: classical quantity is vowel length, which English does not have, so stress stands in for it. The caesura is not checked, and the fifth foot is fixed as a dactyl because a spondaic fifth is rare enough that accepting it would cost more in false positives than it buys.

docs.title: Denckring
docs.text:
denckring · permutation · validated

Five concentric rotating discs of word parts, combined into words by rotation.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Georg Philipp Harsdörffer, Deliciae Physico-Mathematicae (Erquickstunden), part two, Nürnberg 1651, p. 517 — not the Poetischer Trichter, where it is often placed
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind
  • Checkability: self — decidable from the text and its parameters alone
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: both
  • Languages: de
  • Requires: tokens
  • Deterministic: yes
  • In other languages: Fünffacher Denckring der Teutschen Sprache (de), Anneau combinatoire de Harsdörffer (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Harsdörffer labels the rings 48, 50, 12, 120 and 24 but states no total. Two independent counts of the parts disagree about where the boundary between the prefix and suffix rings falls — 49/60/12/120/23 against 48/60/12/120/24 — and both come to 264 parts; both also find 60 on the ring the print labels 50. The 97,209,600 combinations the literature repeats, which go back to Trettien, cannot be right on any of these counts: the figure factors as 2^8 x 3 x 5^2 x 61 x 83, and neither 61 nor 83 divides any ring size. Figures given here are computed from the parts rather than quoted.

docs.title: Prompt hint

docs.title: Haikuization
docs.text:
haikuization · word · validated

A reduction that keeps only the rhyme-words or line ends of an existing poem, leaving a shorter poem inside the longer one.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Oulipo, La Littérature potentielle (1973)
  • Attribution: reference — attested in a standard reference rather than traced to an origin
  • Checkability: source — decidable against the source text it was made from
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: both
  • Languages: en, de
  • Requires: tokens
  • Deterministic: yes
  • In other languages: Haikuisierung (de), Haïkuisation (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Only the line-end reading is checked. The definition's "rhyme-words or line ends" reads as two readings, but this codebase's rhyme machinery always resolves to a line's final word regardless of whether it pronounces as a rhyme with anything else — rhyme_keys hands back that word whether or not two lines' keys ever intersect — so a rhyme-word reading distinct from the line-end reading is not constructible here. phonemes was added to requires in an earlier correction on the assumption the two readings could be told apart; they cannot, so that correction is reversed and this row runs on tokens alone. German declared: borderline, recorded rather than silently assumed. The name evokes a Japanese form neither language's version actually is — what "haikuization" checks is the Oulipo reduction (keep each line's last word, discard the rest), a purely positional operation on line ends that reads and means the same thing whichever language the source poem is in. The name's cultural loading is cosmetic, not part of what is checked.

docs.title: Hemeling's letter-exchange
docs.text:
hemeling · letter · validated

An anagram of a name, explicated beneath it in rhymed verse. Both halves are checked: the first line must use exactly the letters of the source, and the lines under it must hold a rhyme scheme.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Johann Hemeling, Arithmetische Letter- oder BuchstabWechslung (1653); read here through Andreas B. Kilcher, mathesis und poiesis (Fink, 2003), p. 376
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind
  • Checkability: source — decidable against the source text it was made from
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: restrictive
  • Languages: en, de
  • Requires: tokens, fold_diacritics, phonemes
  • Deterministic: yes
  • In other languages: Hemelings Buchstabwechslung (de), Échange de lettres de Hemeling (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The tightest rule in the surveyed European material, because both halves are mechanically checkable where most combinatorial procedures have one half that is not. Hemeling's title says so directly: the anagrams are to be made "und durch Reime zu erklähren". He also specifies a Buchstabenwechsel-Tafel pre-computing combinations up to six elements, played across with lettered dice, and notes that as elements are added the count grows unmanageably — the source itself frames combinatorial explosion as a constraint on the method. Neither the tafel nor the dice are implemented here; only the rule is. The primary text has not been consulted directly. Kilcher, who read it, is named in the source for that reason.

docs.title: Prompt hint
docs.text: Rearrange the letters of a name into a new phrase, then explain the phrase in rhyming lines beneath it.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Default Description allow_identical boolean False Permit a word to rhyme with itself, as French rime riche does. fold_diacritics boolean True Treat accented letters as their base letter, and ß as ss. scheme string AA Rhyme pattern the explication must hold, one letter per line. source string — The text this one was made from. unknown_rhyme string undecidable What a line ending absent from the pronouncing dictionary means: leave the pair unscored (undecidable), let it satisfy the scheme (free), or fail it (strict).

docs.title: Idea-dicing
docs.text:
ideenwuerfeln · procedural · validated

Draw several excerpts from distant fields, filed under one headword, and set them side by side so that a likeness has to be found between them. The checker verifies that the excerpts come from the corpus, that they are filed under the headword asked for, and that they come from different fields when that is required. Whether the collision produced anything is not a question code answers.

docs.title: Provenance

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Jean Paul named the notebook but never wrote the rule down: unlike Harsdörffer, Llull and Kircher, who set out their own procedures, everything here is inferred from the object, and the entry carries reconstruction for that reason. The notebook's numbered sections give way to an alphabetical run of headwords, under which sit remote materials — Roman antiquity, anatomy, entomology, bare aphorisms — with fractional numbers pointing back into the excerpt books, and an occasional mark against what deserved working up. No corpus travels with this package: the manuscripts are public domain, but the transcriptions that make them usable are scholarly editions with their own rights.

docs.text: No acceptance criterion exists. Register and period are properties of usage rather than of form. Deciding this needs two judgements at once: that the content survived, which is the translation problem, and that the register moved, which no lexicon encodes. docs.title: Llullian figure
docs.text:
llull_figure · permutation · validated

A rotating figure of concentric discs bearing the nine dignities, whose turning produces every pairing and triplet of them for contemplation.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Ramon Llull, Ars Generalis Ultima (1305)
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind
  • Checkability: self — decidable from the text and its parameters alone
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: both
  • Languages: en
  • Requires: tokens
  • Deterministic: yes
  • Also known as: figura universalis, volvelle
  • In other languages: Lullische Figur (de), Figure lullienne (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The ternary Ars is implemented; the earlier quaternary phase carries sixteen dignities rather than nine. Counts here are computed from the letters — 84 chambers of three, 36 of two — and the scholarship corroborates both: the tabula runs 84 columns by 20 rows, whose 1,680 cells match the count reported for the Tabula generalis. The 36 binary compartments belong to the third figure, not to Figura A, which is the circle of the nine dignities themselves; an earlier note here misattributed them. No facsimile has been collated. A figure of 504 met in the secondary literature is 9 × 8 × 7, the ordered triples — Llull's chambers are unordered, which is why 84 is the number. Eco's point is worth keeping in view: the wheels do not freely generate new truths, since the stock of principles is fixed and heterodox combinations are excluded elsewhere in the Ars. The reading of the figure as a first computer (Künzel and Bexte, 1989) is reception, not a finding about the object.

docs.title: Prompt hint
docs.text: Take the nine dignities and write out each pairing the wheels bring together.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Default Description arity integer 3 Principles per chamber. figure string llull_ternary Which figure to read against. level — None Which table to read the letters at; inferred if unset.

docs.title: Poetry automat
docs.text:
poesie_automat · permutation · validated

A flap-board of six lines by six modules by ten alternatives, composing a six-line poem at the push of a button — ten to the thirty-sixth of them. The checker asks whether a given poem is one the board admits: each line is cut into its six modules and every piece must be one of that module's ten alternatives.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Hans Magnus Enzensberger, Einladung zu einem Poesie-Automaten (conceived 1974); machine realised for Lyrik am Lech, Landsberg am Lech, 2000
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind
  • Checkability: self — decidable from the text and its parameters alone
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: both
  • Languages: de
  • Requires: —
  • Deterministic: yes
  • Also known as: Poesieautomat, Einladung zu einem Poesie-Automaten
  • In other languages: Landsberger Poesieautomat (de), Automate à poésie (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Six lines, six modules, ten alternatives: 10^36, and all four numbers are stated by the German Wikipedia article on the Landsberger Poesieautomat. The figure is recomputed from the shipped modules rather than quoted, and it is an integer — metrics["combinations"] is a float and cannot hold it exactly. No lexicon of Enzensberger's ships here. He died in 2022, so his word lists are in copyright until 2092; the mechanism is not, and it is the mechanism this row catalogues. The 360 fillers in data/devices/poesieautomat_2000.yaml were written for this project without reference to his lists, on the same footing as the substitute strips the cent_mille_milliards fixture carries for Queneau. How they were made is what can be said; word-for-word non-overlap with a list this project has never read could not be checked, and is not claimed. Three design rules are what make every one of the 10^36 readings grammatical German rather than most of them: the article is folded into the noun so agreement never crosses a module boundary, everything after the subject is an adjunct, and every verb is intransitive third person singular present. Lines 2, 4 and 6 carry no predicate at all, which the sources give as the feature that made the automat programmable in the first place. Grammaticality is a property of the module design and is verified by reading generated poems, not by the checker: check asks only whether a poem is one the board admits.

docs.title: Prompt hint
docs.text: Write six lines of six blocks each; after the subject everything is an adjunct, and every verb is intransitive third person singular present.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Default Description device string poesieautomat_2000 Which device to read the modules from.

docs.title: Proteus verse
docs.text:
proteus_verse · permutation · validated

A line whose words can be permuted into many metrically valid variants. The checker asks two things of a line: that it scans as written, and that its words admit at least a given number of orderings that also scan.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Julius Caesar Scaliger, Poetices libri septem (1561)
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind
  • Checkability: self — decidable from the text and its parameters alone
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: both
  • Languages: en, de
  • Requires: tokens, syllables.heuristic, stress
  • Deterministic: yes
  • In other languages: Proteusvers (de), Vers protée (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Harsdörffer states 39,916,800 permutations for an eleven-word line, which is 11! exactly, and Leibniz takes the figure up in De Arte Combinatoria (1666). It is one of the few counts in this field that can be recomputed from the elements and comes out right. The scanning counts are a different matter: for Bauhusius's hexameter to the Virgin, Puteanus printed 1,022 in 1617, Prestet 2,196 in 1675, Wallis 3,096 in 1685, Leibniz 2,580 in 1686, Bernoulli 3,312 in 1692. They disagree over the ruleset, not the arithmetic, which is why the ruleset is a parameter here and the count a metric rather than a number this row asserts. Knuth gives the history in The Art of Computer Programming 7.2.1.7.

docs.title: Prompt hint

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Default Description max_words integer 9 Refuse a line longer than this rather than search it. metre string hexameter Which measure the permutations must hold: hexameter, iambic_pentameter, iambic_tetrameter, trochaic_tetrameter. minimum integer 2 How many valid orderings the line must admit, itself included.

Heureux qui, comme Ulysse, a fait un beau voyage,

Et puis est retourné, plein d'usage et raison,
Vivre entre ses parents le reste de son aage !
Quand reverray-je, helas, de mon petit village

Que des palais Romains le front audacieux,

docs.title: shakespeare-sonnet-18
docs.text:
en — this text does not satisfy the procedure.

Shall I compare thee to a Summers day?
Thou art more louely and more temperate:
Rough windes do shake the darling buds of Maie,
And Sommers lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heauen shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd,
And euery faire from faire some-time declines,
By chance, or natures changing course vntrim'd:
But thy eternall Sommer shall not fade,
Nor loose possession of that faire thou ow'st,
Nor shall death brag thou wandr'st in his shade,
When in eternall lines to time thou grow'st,
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
So long liues this, and this giues life to thee.

Source: William Shakespeare, Sonnets (1609), no. 18, based on Shake-speares Sonnets (London: Thomas Thorpe, 1609), the 1609 Quarto; original spelling, long-s normalised to s (ADR 0040 D5 — transcribed as printed, not modernised). Rejected: temperate/date is an Elizabethan rhyme this package's strict rhyme model does not accept (does_not_rhyme, ADR 0040 D3), the same pairing gives wrong_stress on "temperate" (100 vs expected 101), and three lines carrying 1609 spellings the pronouncing dictionary does not hold — "heauen", "vntrim'd", "wandr'st" — fall through to a fallback count that reads 9 syllables instead of 10 (wrong_line_length). Measured on this HEAD: score 0.9615, 5 violations.

docs.text:

Du sihst/ wohin du sihst nur Eitelkeit auff Erden.
Was dieser heute baut/ reist jener morgen ein:
Wo itzund Städte stehn/ wird eine Wiesen seyn/
Auff der ein Schäfers-Kind wird spielen mit den Herden.
Was itzund prächtig blüht/ sol bald zutretten werden.
Was itzt so pocht vnd trotzt ist morgen Asch vnd Bein/
Nichts ist/ das ewig sey/ kein Ertz/ kein Marmorstein.
Itzt lacht das Glück vns an/ bald donnern die Beschwerden.
Der hohen Thaten Ruhm muß wie ein Traum vergehn.
Soll denn das Spiel der Zeit/ der leichte Mensch bestehn?
Ach! was ist alles diß/ was wir vor köstlich achten/
Als schlechte Nichtigkeit/ als Schatten/ Staub vnd Wind;
Als eine Wiesen-Blum/ die man nicht wider find't.

At large of good which there by me was found,
I will relate what other things befell.

Source: Dante, Inferno, Canto I, lines 1-9; English terza-rima translation by James Romanes Sibbald, The Divine Comedy of Dante Alighieri (Edinburgh: David Douglas, 1884). Rejected: Sibbald's rhyme is genuinely interlocking (ABA BCB CDC) but two of its three chains rhyme on slant or eye-rhyme rather than a rhyme this package's strict model accepts — "renewed" does not rhyme with either "wood" or "understood", and "terrible" does not rhyme with "tell" or "befell" (does_not_rhyme, ADR 0040 D3). Measured on this HEAD: score 0.8889, 4 violations.

tmesis · syntax · validated

A text that splits a word in two and inserts other material between the halves, as in "abso-bloody-lutely".

docs.title: Provenance

  • Requires: tokens, lexicon.words
  • Deterministic: yes

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: German declared on what the checker actually tests: a hyphen-joined run whose outer parts rejoin as a lexicon word. German compounding gives that operation more material than English does — Fern-seltsam-seher splits Fernseher at a real seam — so the mechanism transfers even though the definition's example quotes an English colloquial idiom. Separable-verb prefixes are the other thing called tmesis in German grammatical description, and they are outside this row: er machte die Tür auf carries no hyphen, so the checker does not see it and reports too_few_splits. Deciding that case needs the part-of-speech capability no pack provides, the same one homosyntaxism is blocked on.

docs.title: Word ladder
docs.text:
word_ladder · word · validated

A chain of words in which each step changes exactly one letter of the word before it, every step being itself a word.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
• Source: Lewis Carroll, Doublets, a Word Puzzle (1879)
  • Attribution: primary — a named author, work and year this catalogue stands behind
  • Checkability: self — decidable from the text and its parameters alone
  • Attested: author-stated — the originator set this rule down

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Kind: both
  • Languages: en, de, fr
  • Requires: tokens, alphabet, fold_diacritics, lexicon.words
  • Deterministic: yes
  • Also known as: doublets, word golf
  • In other languages: Wortleiter (de), Échelle de mots (fr)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: German and French are declared, and the checker takes a fold_diacritics parameter so both declarations hold. Folded — the house default — schon and schön are the same word and the step is rightly refused; unfolded, they differ in exactly one letter and the canonical German doublet is accepted. French raises the identical question with cote/côte and sur/sûr, and the same parameter answers it the same way. The generator substitutes over alphabet() widened by vowels(), which is how it reaches ä, ö and ü at all; ß is in neither, so apply cannot produce Maße from Masse although check accepts that step unfolded.

docs.title: Prompt hint
docs.text: Move from the first word to the last, changing one letter at a time, each step a real word.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Name Type Default Description fold_diacritics boolean True Treat accented letters as their base letter, and ß as ss. target — None The word apply searches a ladder toward.

docs.title: The whole thing, in forty seconds
docs.text:
The catalogue, every machine on the stage being driven, and a local model checking and generating through this package's own MCP server.

Recorded against a real Chromium and a real server by apps/explorer/tests/browser/overview-gif.mjs, and assembled by scripts/build_overview_gif.py. Nothing in it is staged: the verdicts are the library's own, and the two tool calls at the end were made by gemma4:e4b-it-q4_K_M running on the machine that recorded it, against denckring-mcp over stdio.

The three parts:

The board. All 156 catalogued rows, with the golden cases each one carries and — in red — what an unimplemented row is waiting for.

The stage. Nine machines, each 1280×720, and each one actually turned rather than photographed: the rings spin and stagger inward, the blades cut, the 426 flaps clatter, the ladder's rungs arrive one by one, and the calculator turns over. Ideenwürfeln throws three excerpts filed under control from three distinct fields — fluid dynamics, soft matter, and the epidemiology of rabies — which is the collision the procedure exists for. The machines are: Harsdörffer's Denckring, Jean Paul's excerpt boxes, N+7, Queneau's Cent mille milliards, Carroll's Doublets, the cut-up, a Llullian figure, Enzensberger's Poesie-Automat, and a pocket calculator turned upside down.

Over MCP. check_text on a German calculator word, then apply_procedure on an English anagram, with the raw JSON the server sent back.
